**0:14** · Let’s start with the tiny dust mite.

### Bed bugs

**3:24** · These bed bugs are after your blood and they go for it while you’re sleeping.

**3:29** · Keep watching to see how researchers stop them dead in their tracks.

**3:35** · Good night, sleep tight, don’t let the … OK, you know where this is going.

**3:54** · ... to bed bug chow time.

**3:58** · You won’t even feel it.

**4:28** · Until you get … You can recognize them by their signature work of art.

**4:50** · It’s the digested blood they leave behind.

**4:54** · In the 1950s, we made bed bugs retreat with DDT.

**5:27** · Watch this.

**5:36** · This bean leaf can incapacitate the bloodsuckers.

**7:05** · In the meantime, bed bugs are still a step ahead. So keep an eye out.

### Termites

**7:19** · Termites can infiltrate your home without being seen, and the results can be catastrophic.

**7:25** · But these tiny homewreckers wouldn’t be able to do so much damage without the help of special microorganisms hidden in their gut.

**7:36** · That lump on the side of this tree in the Amazon?

**7:39** · It's packed with termites. In the rainforest, that's a good thing.

**7:45** · They break down wood into stuff other creatures can eat.

**7:48** · But inside our homes, termites are pests. They cost us billions of dollars of damage every year.

**7:55** · Take these dampwood termites that live on the cool California coast.

**7:59** · They eat wood that’s wet or decayed, maybe from a leak in your house.

**8:05** · Slowly, but surely, they gnaw and scrape away.

**8:10** · What comes out the other end isn’t waste.

**8:16** · It serves as a kind of mortar.

**8:20** · And dried poop pellets make perfect building blocks for their nests.

**8:25** · In other words, they’re turning your house into theirs.

**8:29** · What’s amazing is that they can digest wood, which is so hard, and get nutrients out of it.

**8:35** · We certainly can’t do that.

**8:37** · Termites are one of the only animals that can.

**8:40** · It turns out they don’t do this alone.

**8:43** · Researchers are looking inside termites to figure out who’s actually responsible for this feat.

**8:49** · At the Exploratorium, in San Francisco, museum biologists give the insect a little puff of carbon dioxide.

**8:57** · When it’s nice and relaxed, the termite poops itself.

**9:03** · Under the microscope, multitudes appear.

**9:07** · Hundreds of species of microbes live packed inside a termite’s gut, about one one-thousandth of a teaspoon.

**9:14** · This big one is called Trichonympha.

**9:17** · It’s not an animal, plant or fungus. It’s a protist.

**9:21** · Watch it move with the help of its flagella.

**9:26** · Protists like Trichonympha are essential for termites to turn the wood into a source of energy.

**9:31** · They do this by fermenting the wood, much the same way a brewer turns grain into beer.

**9:38** · Something else is hidden deep in the termite’s gut.

**9:41** · A powerful bacterium that combines nitrogen from the air and calories from the wood to make protein.

**9:48** · That’s like turning a potato into a steak.

**9:51** · Termites can’t live without their microbes.

**9:53** · And many of these microbes can’t live outside the termite.

**9:57** · So what if we used the microbes against their hosts?

**10:01** · Right now, when we want to get rid of termites, we fumigate our houses with poison.

**10:08** · But maybe we could just kill the protists instead.

**10:11** · Louisiana State University entomologists are engineering a gut bacterium to kill gut protists.

**10:18** · They’d sneak the bacteria into the termite colony on something the termites would eat.

**10:24** · The bacteria would kill the protists that help the termites digest wood, leaving them surrounded by food but starving.

### Drain flies

**10:42** · These cuties are experts in making their way into your house through some secret and slimy passageways.

**10:50** · Check it out.

**10:54** · Ever wonder where those little insects crawling around your bathroom came from?

**11:00** · Bad news: your drain.

**11:05** · With all that fluffy hair, it looks like a tiny moth.

**11:12** · And some do call it a moth fly.

**11:15** · But a fly it is.

**11:18** · A drain fly.

**11:20** · It’s called Clogmia – how appropriate.

**11:24** · It grew up over several weeks, out of sight, among things you thought you’d washed away.

**11:33** · Drain flies sneak in from the outside, through a crack in an old pipe, for example, to sip some water they sensed with this long mustache – their maxillary palps.

**11:47** · And here, on the plentiful gunk in your pipes, they’ll grow a family.

**11:52** · Welcome, little one!

**11:54** · The larva is the length of an eyelash.

**11:58** · That gunk it lives in? Those are bits of you: hair, saliva and food.

**12:04** · They make a nice meal for bacteria and fungi, which form this dark, living slime called a biofilm.

**12:13** · This is what the larvae feed on.

**12:17** · It also keeps them well moisturized.

**12:21** · If the larva ends up submerged, it can still chow down.

**12:27** · It sweeps slime particles out of the water with a hairy mouthpart called the labrum.

**12:37** · And rakes them in with its mandibles.

**12:44** · Underwater, it breathes with a bubble on its backside that it collected at the surface.

**12:52** · This allows it to venture through deep pools in your pipes.

**12:56** · When larvae, or the more grown-up pupae, like this guy here, end up in a toilet bowl, it can be a shock.

**13:06** · You might think the squigglers came out of you!

**13:10** · Ew!

**13:11** · Don’t worry – they can’t live inside us.

**13:15** · And even though the drain flies in your bathroom muck around in bacteria, they don’t really spread it to humans.

**13:23** · They’re not interested in landing on us. Or even leaving the bathroom.

**13:27** · They’re in their happy place.

**13:30** · When you wash your hands?

**13:32** · They protect themselves from the water with their hairy wings.

**13:37** · Each hair has ridges that trap air so the drops roll right off.

**13:47** · And if they’re caught off-guard by a sudden surge, the flies skate across.

**13:56** · But they’re not invincible.

**13:59** · When they get trapped underwater long enough, they can drown.

**14:06** · If you find you really need to get rid of them, drain cleaner helps, but it won’t keep them away forever.

**14:13** · There will always be some slime left behind, deep in your pipes, that could attract the flies again.

**14:21** · So, if they want it, why not let ‘em have it?

### Cockroaches

**14:26** · Are cockroaches – those disgusting disease-spreading roommates – good for anything at all?

**14:32** · [hitting wood] [hitting floor] Scientists think their super-strength might teach us some tricks that could someday save lives.

**14:41** · The American cockroach is one of the fastest insects on the planet.

**14:47** · It can run up to 3.4 miles per hour.

**14:51** · That’d be like a human knocking out eight marathons over their lunch break.

**14:58** · It uses hooks, called tarsal claws, to flip over ledges.

**15:02** · [cymbal ta-da] [cymbal ta-da] And not even a wall can stop it.

**15:21** · Better to keep up the momentum and figure it out as you go.

**15:28** · The roach is both tough and flexible.

**15:32** · Its exoskeleton isn’t one large piece of armor, but many shield-like plates made of a tough material called chitin.

**15:42** · They’re held together by lots of pliable joints.

**15:46** · And they use all those bendy joints to fold up, origami-style, and push through impossibly small cracks … ... like that gap you never knew existed in your kitchen cupboard.

**16:02** · The cockroach can army-crawl through a space a quarter of its normal standing height.

**16:09** · That's one reason it's so good at surviving your thwack.

**16:15** · So how much pressure can the cockroach take?

**16:19** · Scientists at UC Berkeley found it can withstand a thwack ...

**16:24** · ... equivalent to 900 times its body weight … … and walk away unscathed.

**16:32** · Why are researchers so interested in all this?

**16:35** · They think the roach, despite its ability to make us sick, can teach us to save lives.

**16:43** · One of those researchers is now building robots the size of insects to squeeze into places you and I cannot.

**16:52** · Like piles of rubble left by major earthquakes or hurricanes.

**17:00** · And maybe down the line, much smaller versions of these robots could even enter our bodies to perform life-saving tasks.

**17:11** · On the one hand, we want to keep these creatures out ...

**17:14** · by sealing cracks, caulking windows and storing food in airtight containers.

**17:20** · But we also want to learn from them.

**17:24** · The cockroach teaches us that the key to overcoming adversity isn't just toughness.

**17:30** · It’s also flexibility.
